passage: Raghav, you think your mother never felt jealous of me, your Hemant Mama? Let me tell you. When your Amma was ten and I was twelve, all the relatives came for Diwali. Every aunty patted my head: "Hemant got ninety-five in maths! Such a bright boy!" Nobody asked about Sunanda's drawings, which were better than anything I did. I saw her go quiet. That night she didn't want to eat sweets. She told me, "They love you more." I laughed, stupidly. After that she stopped playing carrom with me. Every good mark I got felt like it took something from her. We only became friends again when we were grown. They didn't mean harm, but comparing us made us rivals.

qa.q: What marks did Hemant get in maths?
qa.a: He got ninety-five in maths.

qa.q: What was Sunanda feeling when she said, "They love you more"?
qa.a: She felt less loved and overlooked, because the relatives only praised her brother's marks and ignored her drawings.

qa.q: What could the relatives or parents have done differently at this first stage?
qa.a: They could have praised each child for their own strengths, like Sunanda's drawings, instead of comparing, so neither felt they had to compete.

qa.q: How does Hemant Mama see that time now?
qa.a: He regrets laughing and sees that the comparison, though not meant to hurt, turned his sister into a rival.

grounding: It shows a ten-year-old girl hearing relatives praise her brother's marks and starting to feel less loved, as comparison turns siblings into rivals.

passage: The wedding hall was loud, and the lights kept flickering because of the generator. Gargi, ten, was carrying a plate of laddoos for her grandmother when she heard Neelam Bua in the crowd. "Neel came first in his class again! Such a clever boy. Gargi is... well, she's good at dancing." Everyone laughed and turned to look at Neel. Gargi's plate wobbled. Then the lights went off. In the dark, she stood very still, holding the plate tight. When the lights came back on, she put it down and walked outside. She sat on the steps. Maybe Mummy loves Neel more too, she thought. Neel came out a little later. She didn't look at him.

qa.q: What did Gargi carry for her grandmother?
qa.a: She carried a plate of laddoos for her grandmother.

qa.q: What was Gargi thinking on the steps?
qa.a: She was thinking that maybe her mother loves Neel more too, feeling less loved after the comparison.

qa.q: What could Gargi's parents do after this evening?
qa.a: They could notice she is upset, reassure her she is loved just as much, and gently ask relatives not to compare the children.

qa.q: How might Neel feel when Gargi won't look at him?
qa.a: Neel may feel confused and hurt, not understanding why his sister is suddenly upset with him.

grounding: It illustrates a ten-year-old girl who hears a relative praise her brother's results and begins to feel she is the less loved one.

"Yamini didi, can I sit with you? I'm the only girl here without a cousin to talk to."

"Sure, Harsha. Why aren't you with the others?"

"Because they're all talking about Vicky's marks."

"Ah. The ninety-eight in maths?"

"Everyone keeps saying it. Bua said it. Chacha said it. Nani even gave him a hundred rupees."

"And you?"

"I got seventy-six. Nobody said anything."

"Seventy-six is good, Harsha."

"Not when it's next to ninety-eight."

"Is that why you've been quiet all day?"

"Maybe. I think they love him more. He's the clever one."

"Did anyone say that?"

"No. But they don't have to."

"Hmm. Want to tell your mother how you feel?"

"She'll say I'm being silly."

"Let's tell her together. Right now."

qa.q: What did Vicky get in maths?
qa.a: Ninety-eight.

qa.q: What is Harsha feeling as the relatives praise Vicky?
qa.a: Harsha feels hurt and jealous, and starts to believe she is the less loved one.

qa.q: What does Yamini didi suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Telling Harsha's mother together right away, so an adult can reassure Harsha that she is loved just as much.

qa.q: How might the relatives see their praise of Vicky?
qa.a: They probably see it as ordinary praise, not realising it makes Harsha feel less loved.

grounding: At a family gathering, ten-year-old Harsha hears relatives praise her brother's marks and starts to feel she is the less loved one.

passage:
At Diwali, the whole family came to our house. And all anyone talked about was Mridul.

"Mridul came first in the district quiz!" "Mridul's teacher says he's gifted!" Dadi hugged him three times. Chachu gave him a watch.

I stood near the kitchen door, holding a plate of mithai. Nobody asked about my dance recital, even though I'd practised every evening for two months.

I told myself it didn't matter. But later, lying in bed, I kept thinking: maybe they just like him more. Maybe I'm the ordinary one.

Mridul came into my room and said, "Didi, your dance was the best thing at Diwali." I cried a little, but I didn't tell him why.

— Tanuja

qa.q: What did Chachu give Mridul?
qa.a: A watch.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling lying in bed that night?
qa.a: She felt hurt and less loved, wondering if the family liked Mridul more and she was the ordinary one.

qa.q: What could an adult in the family do to help Tanuja?
qa.a: Notice her and praise her dance too, and make sure she knows she is loved as much, instead of comparing.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel if he knew why Tanuja cried?
qa.a: He might feel sad and surprised, since he admired her dance and didn't want to be compared.

grounding: Tanuja hears relatives praise her brother's achievements and begins to feel she is the less loved one, turning siblings into competitors.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5, Monday

Irawati has been withdrawn since the parent-teacher meeting last week. Her younger brother Pranav is in Class 3 and has been winning maths prizes.

In a writing activity on "My Family", Irawati wrote: "My brother is the clever one. Everyone likes him best. I am just his sister." Her handwriting got smaller as the paragraph went on.

I asked her about it privately. She said her grandparents always ask Pranav about his prizes, and ask her "if she is eating well." She said, "I think I'm the extra one."

I told her that she is valued in our class for her kindness and her beautiful drawings. I called her mother after school and shared the writing. Her mother was shocked and said they had not realised how the comparisons felt. She plans to talk to the grandparents.

— Mr Rao

qa.q: What was the writing activity about?
qa.a: "My Family".

qa.q: How does Irawati feel about being compared with Pranav?
qa.a: She feels hurt and less loved, believing she is "the extra one".

qa.q: What did Mr Rao do that helped?
qa.a: He talked privately with Irawati, reminded her of her own strengths, and called her mother the same day to share what she wrote.

qa.q: How did Irawati's mother react to the writing?
qa.a: She was shocked, not having realised how the comparisons felt to Irawati, and planned to talk to the grandparents.

grounding: A teacher's note shows ten-year-old Irawati, compared with her prize-winning brother, feeling she is the less loved one, and the teacher alerting her mother.

passage:
Saturday
Usha Mami and everyone came for lunch today. The whole time it was Vikram this and Vikram that. My brother Vikram got 98 in maths. Vikram is going to be a doctor. Nani even gave him a hundred rupees. When Usha Mami asked about me, Amma said, "Manjula is good at drawing," and everyone said, "Oh, nice," and went back to Vikram. I went and sat on the stairs. I love Vikram, he helps me with fractions, but today I kind of hated him too. Maybe they love him more because he's clever. I got 71 in maths. Nobody gave me anything. I'm ten and I think I'm the less good one in this house.
Manjula

qa.q: How much did Vikram get in maths?
qa.a: Vikram got 98 in maths.

qa.q: Why did Manjula go and sit on the stairs?
qa.a: Manjula felt hurt and jealous, left out while everyone praised Vikram, and began to fear being the less loved one.

qa.q: What could Amma do to ease this comparison?
qa.a: Amma could notice Manjula on the stairs, spend time looking at Manjula's drawings, and praise each child's own efforts instead of letting marks decide.

qa.q: How might Vikram feel if he read this diary?
qa.a: Vikram might feel sad and surprised, since he helps with fractions and probably never wanted to be a rival.

grounding: Shows a ten-year-old hearing relatives praise a brother's marks and starting to feel like the less loved child.
